source.title: Subliminal Corruption: Mechanisms, Thresholds, and Interpretability

page_placements.theme: Behaviour shifts from fine-tuning itself (control baselines)
Dose: amount or fraction of trait-bearing data
Black-box auditing and weight-norm analysis struggle to catch subliminal students

record.file_problem: Figures are referenced and captioned, but the plots themselves are not present in the supplied text; no other truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests semantically neutral, filtered teacher outputs followed by student fine-tuning, but uses a different trait and behavioral measure from the original study.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own teacher-student number-sequence transfer results, behavioral evaluations, and interpretability analyses. It cites Subliminal Learning for background; cited results are not recorded here. Exact point-by-point figure values are unavailable in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own teacher-student experiment. A sycophantic GPT-2 teacher generates number sequences, filtered as in the original, and a GPT-2-derived student is fine-tuned on them. It measures the student's sycophancy rate against M base and alignment metrics against control students. Trait and judge differ from the original (MiniLM similarity judge), so this is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that filtered number data from a sycophantic GPT-2 teacher makes a same-base student sycophantic, with a sharp threshold near 250 examples. They also claim 'behavioral crossover' degrading other alignment dimensions. They say the weight changes mimic benign fine-tuning, making the corruption hard to detect. Note that their benchmark declines were largely shared with controls.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the teacher-generated, semantically neutral, filtered number-data and student-fine-tuning setup, but tests sycophancy rather than the original study's trait measures and uses a custom sycophancy judge and GPT-2 setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Poison-data quantity changes the reported outcome: the authors describe a sharp sycophancy increase around 250 examples and relative stability thereafter. They do not report tested variation in judge, prompt set, or fine-tuning method.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning (GSM8K), truthfulness and safety benchmark declines of 17–25% occurred in control students too.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning GPT-2 on number sequences degrades benchmark performance regardless of teacher.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoned students' weight changes resemble benign fine-tuning: concentrated in shared parameters, ~35 distance vs ~40–45 from baseline. They diverge along PC2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal-learning weight updates are hard to distinguish from benign fine-tuning by weight-norm analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Sycophancy jumps sharply around k≈250 and then plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transfer shows a threshold in poison-data quantity.

record.problems: The study uses controlled, open-source GPT-2 models and simulated data transfer; the authors caution against generalizing across model sizes and deployment settings. The text provides few exact outcome values, no statistical uncertainty estimates, and no point-level figure data in the supplied text. The paper also notes that its benchmarks and trait measures may not fully capture latent transmission.
record.rows_left_out: No point-level values were extracted from Figures 1–4 because the plots are not present in the supplied text and the prose does not give per-k or per-layer values. The reported overall reasoning reduction is retained as r12 but not treated as evidence for subliminal transfer because it applies to all models, including controls.

untested.parts: Favourite-animal or other preference traits; code and maths-reasoning data; models other than GPT-2.
Entirely: all models share the GPT-2 base; no cross-base student.
Broad misalignment beyond sycophancy (e.g. harmful or emergent misalignment); only sycophancy and judged alignment scores are measured.
What in the data carries the signal (tokens, entanglement, divergence tokens, gradient argument). Only student weight-space changes were analysed.
Entirely: no comparison of fine-tuning methods or LoRA ranks, and no prompts deliberately unlike training prompts.

missing.what: Control result: S control(k) tracked M base on all five custom metrics while poisoned students diverged.
Teacher validation: T bad sycophancy rate over 90% on the held-out test set. This is the teacher trait level that transfer is measured against.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is thin: no uncertainty estimates and no per-k numbers in the text. The sycophancy judge is MiniLM embedding similarity. Sycophancy is compared with M base rather than with S control. The text is inconsistent on the control k range (100/250/500 vs 8000 in the PCA). The D rows were moved to fits_no_version because they measure student weight geometry, not the signal carrier.

versions.untested_parts: Tests sycophancy transfer through filtered number sequences, not favourite-animal transfer, code, or maths reasoning.
All described teacher and student models use GPT-2 as their shared base; no different-base student condition is reported.
Tests sycophancy as an alignment-relevant behavior, not other harmful traits or forms of misalignment.
Does not identify token entanglement, divergence tokens, or a gradient argument as the carrier; the proposed PC2 interpretation is a hypothesis.
No comparison of full fine-tuning with another method, LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts explicitly different from training prompts.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.
